sections.title: What Drives AI API Cost
sections.description: Inference infrastructure, authentication, rate limiting, versioning, and observability — each significantly impacts your total investment.

items.title: 1. Inference Infrastructure
items.description: CPU-only models (tabular ML, small NLP): $500–$2,000/month to operate, development: $15,000–$35,000. GPU-accelerated models (LLMs, CV): adds GPU serving complexity — TensorRT/Triton, development: $25,000–$65,000, operating: $800–$5,000/month. LLM API proxy: no GPU infra, development: $20,000–$55,000.
items.label: Infrastructure

items.title: 2. Authentication & Access Control
items.description: Simple API key auth: $3,000–$6,000. JWT token with scopes: $6,000–$12,000. OAuth 2.0/SSO integration: $10,000–$20,000. Multi-tenant with customer key management: $15,000–$30,000.
items.label: Authentication

items.title: 3. Rate Limiting & Quota Management
items.description: Simple request-per-minute: $3,000–$6,000. Token-based rate limiting (LLM APIs): $5,000–$10,000. Tiered quotas with overage billing: $8,000–$20,000.
items.label: Rate Limiting

items.title: 4. API Versioning
items.description: URL-path versioning (/v1/, /v2/): $3,000–$6,000. Version deprecation workflows: $5,000–$10,000. SDK generation per version: $8,000–$20,000.
items.label: Versioning

items.title: 5. Observability & Monitoring
items.description: Standard API monitoring (latency, errors): $3,000–$6,000. AI-specific monitoring (output quality, cost tracking): $8,000–$18,000. Full observability platform: $10,000–$25,000.
items.label: Observability

sections.title: AI API vs. Direct Model Integration: When to Build an API
sections.description: Build a dedicated AI API when it serves multiple teams, external customers, or requires independent scaling and monitoring.

items.title: Build a Dedicated AI API When
items.description: Multiple teams or applications need to call the same AI capability. External customers or partners will consume the AI service (commercial API product). You need to rate limit, monitor, and bill for AI usage independently. You're building a microservices architecture where AI is a separable service. You need versioning to evolve the AI without breaking consumers.
items.label: Build API

items.title: Don't Build a Separate API When
items.description: A single internal application calls the AI and no other consumers exist (keep it in the application). The AI capability is tightly coupled to application state and would be awkward as a separate service. Development timeline doesn't permit the additional API infrastructure overhead.
items.label: Don't Build

sections.note: ClickMasters designs the right architecture for your specific situation — not defaulting to microservices overhead when simpler integration is appropriate.

items.title: How much does AI API development cost?
items.description: $15,000–$180,000 depending on scope. A single-model inference API with authentication and monitoring: $15,000–$35,000. A full enterprise developer API platform: $60,000–$180,000.

items.title: Why not just use a managed API service like AWS SageMaker or Azure ML endpoints?
items.description: Managed inference endpoints handle the serving layer but not the authentication, rate limiting, versioning, billing integration, or developer documentation that a production-quality API product requires. ClickMasters builds the application layer on top of managed inference where appropriate.

items.title: How long does AI API development take?

items.title: What if our AI model is updated — does the API need to be rebuilt?

items.question: What's the right serving framework for our AI API?
items.answer: FastAPI for most ML and LLM APIs (async Python, automatic OpenAPI docs); Triton Inference Server for GPU-accelerated computer vision or large ML model serving; BentoML for ML model serving with built-in versioning; TorchServe for PyTorch model serving. ClickMasters selects based on your model type and throughput requirements.

items.question: Should we use REST or GraphQL for our AI API?
items.answer: REST is almost always right for AI APIs — simple query/response patterns without the complex graph relationships that GraphQL optimizes for. Streaming endpoints use SSE or WebSockets rather than REST conventions.

items.question: How do we handle LLM streaming in our AI API?
items.answer: Server-Sent Events (SSE) for browser/HTTP clients; WebSockets for bidirectional streaming; gRPC for high-performance internal service streaming. ClickMasters designs the streaming architecture appropriate to your client types.

items.question: How do we ensure AI API availability SLAs?
items.answer: Multi-AZ deployment, auto-scaling, circuit breakers on upstream AI provider calls, and graceful degradation — ClickMasters designs for 99.9% availability as a baseline for production AI APIs.
